title: How Much Do Two Groups Overlap?
scopeNote: This keeps the original's prediction hook and its live two-curve figure with all four indices. The sample-size control that separates an effect size from a test statistic, the four-index matching challenge and the published-effect presets stay in the longer version, and the page says so.
summary: Guess how much of the lower group still beats the average of the higher group at a large effect, then see it. Two normal curves with their overlap shaded, and Cohen's d, the overlap, the probability of superiority and U3 all describing the same picture.
learningObjectives: Compute Cohen's d from a mean difference and a standard deviation, and explain why it has no units.
Translate an effect size into overlap, probability of superiority and U3.
Recognise how much two distributions still overlap at a conventionally large effect.
Explain why the same d can arise from studies with nothing in common.
State what a group difference does and does not license about an individual.
interactionTypes: a single-best-answer prediction locked in before any figure is shown
explanatory feedback that differs by the direction of the learner's error
two live controls over the gap and the spread
two normal curves with the shared region shaded, updating live
a scale-free demonstration cycling three studies that draw the identical figure
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. Everything is computed in the browser and is gone when the page is closed.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. The prediction options carry a hidden state note as well as a colour and a glyph, so the marked answer is never signalled by colour alone. The two curves differ by dash pattern as well as by colour, and each is labelled on its own outer flank so the labels never collide however small the difference. Labels are drawn with a background-coloured halo so they stay legible over the curves. The figure description gives the difference, the spread and all four indices, so no conclusion depends on reading the curves. The figure scrolls sideways rather than shrinking below legible label sizes on a narrow screen. Changes are announced through a polite live region. No timed content and no motion.
dataStatus: Illustrative. There is no dataset and no sampling: the two curves are normal densities drawn from the difference and spread on screen. No figure is a norm or a published effect.
simulationNotes: No randomness and nothing to seed. All four indices are exact closed forms that hold under the assumption both groups are normal with the same standard deviation: d is the difference over that standard deviation, overlap is twice the normal tail at minus d over two, the probability of superiority is the normal distribution function at d over root two, and U3 is the normal distribution function at d. The activity offers one spread control rather than two precisely because these forms depend on the equal-spread assumption; the caution says what changes when it fails. The axis is deliberately autoscaled and carries no tick values, the opposite decision from the z-score activity and for the opposite reason: here the point is that nothing depends on the units, so any two settings with the same d render an identical figure, which the scale-free control demonstrates directly.
readmeTopic: how much two distributions still overlap at a large effect, and why an effect size says nothing about whether an effect is real
